#9754. GPT-4.5 Fooled 73% of Judges: 20 Turing Tests, Detectors and Fakes to Check Your AI Radar

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

In a 2025 UC San Diego study, people picked GPT-4.5 as the human 73% of the time, more often than they picked the actual humans. ELIZA, a 1960s chatbot, scored 23%, slightly ahead of GPT-4o without a persona at 21%. Here are 20 tests from the Turing Test directory where you can check whether you still tell human from machine across chat, text, faces, art, voice and video.

The Turing test used to be a thought experiment. Now it's a party game, a research method and a product category. Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen's three-party Turing test had 284 participants chat with a human and an AI at the same time and then pick the human. GPT-4.5 with a persona prompt won 73% of the time, and LLaMa-3.1-405B won 56%.

The public versions tell the same story. AI21 Labs' "Human or Not?" game ran more than 10 million conversations, and players guessed right only 68% of the time. They were worse at spotting the bots (60%) than at spotting the humans (73%). And it isn't just chat: in a blind listening study covered on HackerNoon, listeners trying to pick out AI-composed piano music were "essentially guessing," at close to 50% accuracy.

So test yourself. A note on what's included: not everything here is a quiz. Some are games, some are detectors that try to make the call for you, and some are the generators that make the fakes. To understand the Turing test in 2026, you need all three.

1. Human or Not? by AI21 Labs. You get a two-minute chat with a stranger, then guess whether it was a person or a bot. It became the largest Turing test ever run, with more than 1.5 million participants. The research paper breaks down the tricks players used to unmask bots.

2. Loebner Prize. This was the original Turing test competition, held from 1991 according to its Wikipedia history. It's no longer running; its last winner was Mitsuku in 2019. It belongs on any list because it shows how long "fooling the judges" was the goal, and how easy it looks now.

3. Bot or Not (Botometer) by Indiana University's OSoMe. It scores whether a social media account is a bot. It's a Turing test turned into a classifier. The live version shut down after X ended free researcher access, and the Botometer X archive only covers accounts created before June 2023.

4. GLTR (Giant Language model Test Room) from the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab and Harvard NLP. Paste text and it colors each word by how predictable it was to a language model. It was built in 2019 to spot AI-written text, and it's still the best way to see why AI text "feels" smooth.

5. GPTZero. This is the AI-writing detector that teachers made famous. Run your own writing through it to see how often humans get flagged. HackerNoon's guide on how to detect text generated by AI explains what these tools measure.

6. Poem or AI? You read a poem and decide who wrote it. The research on this is humbling: in Porter and Machery's Scientific Reports study, 1,634 readers couldn't reliably tell ChatGPT poems from famous poets', and they rated the AI poems higher.

7. NYT AI Article Quiz by The New York Times. Short passages, one question: human or AI?

8. WritersBrew AI Detector. A writing tool with a built-in check on whether a passage reads as machine-written.

9. Winograd Schema Challenge. This is the benchmark proposed as a better Turing test. Who does "it" refer to in "The trophy doesn't fit in the suitcase because it's too big"? It's easy for people. For years it was hard for machines.

10. Which Face Is Real? by Jevin West and Carl Bergstrom at the University of Washington. You see two faces and click the real one. It logged about 4 million plays in two weeks after its 2019 launch, and players were right about 70% of the time against StyleGAN fakes.

11. This Person Does Not Exist. This is the generator, not the quiz. Every refresh shows a face of someone who was never born. Look at the ears, teeth and backgrounds to learn the tells.

12. Sensity AI. A commercial deepfake detection platform for faces, video and identity fraud. It's what the professionals use when the stakes are higher than a game.

13. AI or Not. Upload an image and get a verdict on whether it's AI-generated. Try it on your own photos first.

14. Artbreeder. A collaborative image generator where you "breed" images by mixing them. Spend ten minutes making fakes and you'll get better at spotting them.

15. MIT GAN Dissect from MIT CSAIL. A research tool that shows which neurons inside a GAN draw trees, doors or clouds, and lets you switch them off. It doesn't test you. It shows you what's inside the machine you're testing.

16. Real or Fake Voice. Listen to clips and decide which are human speech and which are AI voice clones. This one matters most in practice, because voice cloning is the deepfake behind phone scams.

17. AIVA AI Music. An AI music composer. Play its tracks for friends without telling them and see who notices.

18. Deepfake Detection Challenge. The Kaggle competition, organized by Facebook with industry and academic partners, to build automatic deepfake detectors. Its dataset is still a standard for training them.

19. Detective (Deepware). Paste a video link and it scans for face manipulation.

20. FakeApp / Faceswap. The deepfake software that started it all. It's on this list because detectors are trained against it.

The pattern holds across formats. People do only somewhat better than a coin flip at spotting AI, and they get worse as models improve. Faces were about 70% in 2019, chat was 68% in 2023, and by 2025 people were choosing GPT-4.5 over real humans. The Turing test has stopped being a bar for machines to clear. It's turning into a skill humans have to practice.

Browse and filter every test by type (Audio, Classic, Game, Modern LLM, Social, Visual), difficulty and access in the Turing Test directory.

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

#9753. Why High-Frequency Trading (HFT) Firms Still Rely on Bare Metal Over Cloud Servers

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at bytesrack.com

In High-Frequency Trading (HFT), speed is the actual product. A single millisecond delay dictates whether a strategy captures a profit or absorbs a loss.

While streaming platforms, social networks, and retail banks have migrated heavily to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, the HFT sector stubbornly anchors its execution systems to physical hardware. They rely on bare metal.

Understanding why well-funded quantitative firms reject infinite cloud scalability requires looking at physics, predictable execution, and absolute architectural control.

High-Frequency Trading is an algorithmic trading method that utilizes powerful computers to process massive volumes of orders in microseconds or nanoseconds. These strategies capitalize on fleeting market inefficiencies. Because multiple firms often target the same micro-opportunity simultaneously, the firm with the fastest execution architecture captures the trade.

Cloud environments rely on hypervisors to divide physical servers among multiple virtual instances. This virtualization layer introduces overhead and, crucially, jitter—microscopic, unpredictable spikes in network response times.

Bare metal servers eliminate this virtualization layer entirely. Trading algorithms interface directly with physical CPUs and network interface cards (NICs). By utilizing kernel-bypass networking protocols like DPDK, firms route data past the standard operating system stack.

The result is consistently flat, sub-microsecond latency. In HFT, consistent execution predictability matters just as much as raw speed. A highly tuned strategy simply cannot survive random processing delays.

Physical distance equates to latency. Light traveling through a fiber-optic cable takes roughly five microseconds to cover one kilometer. To eliminate this transit delay, HFT firms utilize co-location. They lease rack space directly inside, or immediately adjacent to, the stock exchange's primary data center.

Public cloud regions are strategically built in locations optimized for cheap power and vast physical space, placing them geographically distant from financial matching engines. For latency-arbitrage strategies, that physical distance renders public cloud architecture non-viable.

Public clouds operate as multi-tenant environments. If a neighboring virtual machine suddenly spikes in workload, it competes for shared physical resources like memory bandwidth, CPU cache, and network capacity. This creates the "noisy neighbor" problem.

Average cloud performance may appear sufficient, but a microsecond lag caused by another tenant during high market volatility is catastrophic for an active trading algorithm. Bare metal provides a 100% single-tenant environment. Resource availability remains completely static, guaranteed, and predictable around the clock.

HFT infrastructure requires hyper-specialized hardware modifications. Firms extensively deploy FPGAs (Field Programmable Gate Arrays) to execute tasks like parsing market data and generating orders directly at the silicon level.

Engineers strip down BIOS settings, install proprietary network cards, and frequently deploy heavily overclocked processors. While public cloud vendors offer standard FPGA instances and compute-optimized hardware, they restrict low-level firmware tuning. Bare metal allows trading firms to engineer and optimize their hardware stacks down to the individual component level with absolute autonomy.

Trading firms do not ignore cloud technology entirely; they simply segment their workloads.

Latency-critical execution systems remain strictly on co-located bare metal. However, asynchronous operations run in the cloud. Firms heavily leverage cloud infrastructure for backtesting trading strategies, running intensive historical risk analytics, and storing petabytes of market tick data where microseconds do not impact the bottom line.

The cloud remains unmatched for enterprise flexibility, global scalability, and dynamic cost control. Yet, the high-frequency trading sector plays by a different set of physical rules. When trading profits are won and lost in microseconds, financial firms require zero virtualization overhead, physical proximity to the exchange, entirely dedicated processing resources, and silicon-level hardware customization. Until cloud platforms can engineer solutions that bypass the laws of physics and virtualization limits, bare metal will remain the absolute standard for latency-critical market operations.

#9752. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9749. How to fix "SPF permerror: too many DNS lookups"

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at imageconvert.art • AI-assisted

SPF has a hard limit: checking your record may take no more than 10 DNS lookups. Go over it and the result is permerror, which many receivers treat as a failed SPF check, so your mail is more likely to land in spam. It usually creeps up on you as you add more services that send email for you.

Count every include, a, mx, ptr and exists, then repeat for each included domain. Or paste your domain into a checker that does it for you, like this free SPF & DMARC check. If the top level is already close to 10, the includes inside it almost certainly push you over.

DMARC passes if either SPF or DKIM passes and aligns with your domain. Setting up DKIM for every service that sends as you makes SPF less critical, and some services can't be added to SPF at all without going over the limit.

Quick end-to-end test: send yourself an email in Gmail, open it, choose Show original, and look for PASS next to SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

#9747. Tu contraseña es débil: cómo funciona un ataque de fuerza bruta (y cómo defenderte)

Imagina un candado de bicicleta con una combinación de 4 dígitos. ¿Cuántas combinaciones posibles hay? Diez mil: de 0000 a 9999. Si pudieras probar una por segundo, en menos de tres horas lo abrirías… pero una computadora no prueba una por segundo: prueba miles de millones por segundo. Esa es, en esencia, la fuerza bruta: no adivinar con ingenio, sino probar todo, rapidísimo, hasta que algo abra.

Cuando un servicio en internet sufre una filtración, los atacantes no obtienen tu contraseña escrita en claro (o no deberían): obtienen su «hash», una especie de huella digital calculada con una función matemática de un solo sentido. No se puede revertir, pero sí se puede comparar: si calculo el hash de «contraseña123» y coincide con el de la filtración, ya sé tu contraseña.

Y ahí empieza la fiesta para el atacante:

La seguridad de una contraseña no depende de lo «rara» que se vea, sino de cuántas posibilidades debe explorar el atacante, y eso depende de su longitud y del alfabeto usado. Una contraseña de 8 caracteres en minúsculas tiene unos 200 mil millones de combinaciones: suena mucho, pero un equipo moderno de tarjetas gráficas las recorre en horas si el hash es rápido y débil. Una de 16 caracteres con mayúsculas, minúsculas, números y símbolos pasa a un espacio tan grande que ni con siglos de cómputo se recorre.

Por eso una frase larga y memorable — varias palabras unidas, como las que usarías en una historia absurda — suele proteger más que una clave corta llena de símbolos imposibles de recordar.

El ataque más exitoso ni siquiera rompe tu contraseña: la recicla. Si usas la misma clave en el foro que se filtró en 2019 y en tu correo, el atacante solo tiene que probar esa combinación correo+contraseña en todos los servicios conocidos. Se llama credential stuffing y funciona porque millones de personas reutilizan claves.

La fuerza bruta es el ataque menos elegante y uno de los más efectivos, porque no ataca a la tecnología: ataca nuestros atajos. La buena noticia es que la defensa también es matemática y está de tu lado: cada carácter extra que agregas, el atacante lo paga con años.

José Ángel Maldonado Guzmán — estudiante de Ingeniería en Computación, Universidad Autónoma del Estado de México, Centro Universitario Valle de Chalco.

#9744. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9743. A 23M-Parameter Model Still Wins: 338 Embedding Models Ranked by Real Downloads

We publish the best academic papers on rule-based techniques, LLMs, & the generation of text that resembles human text.

We publish the best academic papers on rule-based techniques, LLMs, & the generation of text that resembles human text.

We publish the best academic papers on rule-based techniques, LLMs, & the generation of text that resembles human text.

all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a 23M-parameter sentence-transformers model, was downloaded 177M times on Hugging Face in the last 30 days. That's 38% of all downloads across the 213 open-weight embedding models tracked by the TextModels directory, and more than the next four models combined. Below are all 338 embedding models in the directory: open weights ranked by downloads, then hosted APIs, Ollama builds and the historical models that started it all.

Most "best embedding model" lists rank by benchmark score, like PremAI's ranking by MTEB score, cost and self-hosting. Benchmarks tell you what's best on paper. Downloads tell you what developers actually ship, and the two lists look very different.

The sentence-transformers family's lead has a history. As HackerNoon's overview of embeddings for RAG puts it, "Simply said, the BERT model isn't the best for similarity search." SBERT fixed that by embedding each sentence separately so vectors can be computed once and compared fast, and its descendants still dominate the download charts.

Everything comes from the TextModels directory's Embedding filter (338 models) as of November 11, 2026. Hugging Face entries are ranked by 30-day downloads pulled from the Hugging Face API. "Verified" means the TextModels directory fetched and confirmed that model's metrics per model. Hosted API models have no public download counts, so they're grouped by provider, alphabetically. Some hosted entries, like OpenAI's 001-series search models, are long retired. They stay in the list because people still search for them when migrating old pipelines.

These are models you call over an API instead of downloading. The list covers current models and retired ones still found in old codebases.

248. textembedding-gecko-multilingual@001

Ollama doesn't publish download counts, so these are sorted from smallest to largest. Pick the smallest one that clears your quality bar.

285. qwen3-embedding 0.6b (Alibaba / Qwen)

288. nomic-embed-text-v2-moe latest (size not listed)

Before sentence-transformers there were word vectors, and before RAG there was semantic search. These are the ancestors of everything above.

289. word2vec Skip-gram Google News (Google)

297. GloVe Twitter 27B 200d (Stanford NLP)

298. GloVe Twitter 27B 100d (Stanford NLP)

299. GloVe Twitter 27B 50d (Stanford NLP)

300. GloVe Twitter 27B 25d (Stanford NLP)

301. fastText Common Crawl 300d 2M (Meta AI)

302. fastText Wiki News 300d 1M (Meta AI)

303. ELMo Original 5.5B (Allen Institute for AI)

305. Universal Sentence Encoder DAN (Google)

306. Universal Sentence Encoder Transformer (Google)

320. Sentence-BERT Base NLI Mean Tokens (UKP Lab)

321. Sentence-RoBERTa Large NLI STS-B (UKP Lab)

322. SimCSE BERT Base Supervised (Princeton)

323. SimCSE BERT Base Unsupervised (Princeton)

324. SimCSE RoBERTa Large Supervised (Princeton)

325. SimCSE RoBERTa Base Unsupervised (Princeton)

If you need a default today, the download data points to all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or bge-small-en-v1.5 for English, bge-m3 or multilingual-e5 for multilingual, and Qwen3-Embedding for top quality if you have the GPU. Then test on your own data. The model is only half the stack; HackerNoon's guide to choosing a vector database for a production RAG chatbot covers the other half.

To compare all 3,009 text models, including rerankers, classifiers and the LLMs these embeddings feed, browse the TextModels directory.

#9742. Platform Engineering for Service-Based Organizations

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at improving.com

A consultant wraps up a Kubernetes migration task for a financial services client and moves to a new engagement. For the new client, he does the Kubernetes migration again, covering rebuilding CI/CD, observability, and access management from scratch.

The consultant is solving the same problem that three other teams in his organization already solved last quarter for other clients. So, there are three different approaches but no shared patterns or system for anything to compound.

Platform engineering should be an answer to the common tasks engineers are doing. For product companies, it is. Dedicated platform teams, internal developer platforms, golden paths - everything has evolved and matured over time and the results are visible.

Unfortunately, the platform engineering playbook was built around product company assumptions, with internal developers, consistent infrastructures, stable teams and long-lived products.

Service companies have none of this. Your developers are clients’ engineers, your infrastructure changes with every engagement, and your best consultants rotate across projects before any platform adoption can take hold. Service companies need a different model of platform engineering, and in this blog post, we’re going to explore it.

Platform Engineering is evolving fast and so are the conversations around it. Major conferences like KubeCon, a dedicated conference like PlatformCon and a growing community around platform engineering are a proof of it. The community has done serious work in defining what good looks like.

I’ve spoken and attended a lot of sessions on platform engineering, and almost every reference point is a product company. Spotify building Backstage for hundreds of internal engineers. A fintech standardizing deployment pipeline across product teams. A SaaS company reducing onboarding time for developers and so on.

The IDP model at the center of all this is straightforward. Your developers are your users, the platform team provisions environments and golden paths, and adoption improves over time as platform matures. The stack remains the same, problems remain the same, and everything is repeated at scale. Service organizations break this approach.

Your “internal developers” are spread across ten client engagements, each with a different stack, different cloud provider, and different security postures. A consultant who just ramped on a Kubernetes-heavy fintech project moves to a legacy modernization engagement next quarter. The tools, the patterns, the environment, all different. The IDP they used last quarter may be irrelevant on the next project.

Worse, the clients own their infrastructure - some on AWS, some on GCP with ArgoCD already running and some in air-gapped environments with no access to your tools. You’re working inside someone else’s environment, within their constraints, often adapting on the fly. Self-service portals and standardized pipelines solve a problem your organization doesn’t have in the way the model assumes.

The industry isn’t wrong about platform engineering; it’s just that most of it is describing an organization that’s not service based.

If the IDP model doesn’t fit service companies, what does? Well, the answer lies in the focus.

We need to stop trying to standardize the environment and shift to standardizing the approaches.

A product company can build one platform because their developers work in one environment. Service companies don’t have that luxury. But what stays consistent across engagements is how your best consultants think about problems.

That thinking is an asset, and it has a name: Delivery Capital.

It’s the organizational knowledge your consultants build engagement after engagement, the reference architectures, the diagnosed anti-patterns, and the judgment calls that took three failed approaches to get right. Most services companies let it walk out the door every time a consultant rolls off a project. The capability layer is simply the system that keeps it, and makes it reusable for the next person who needs it.

In practice, this means building two distinct internal layers.

The capability layer is your organizational memory: a platform engineering capability model covering the patterns, approaches, and decisions your consultants shouldn't have to rebuild from scratch for every engagement.

Everything that was done for every engagement becomes a part of your capability layer.

When a consultant starts a new Kubernetes migration, they don’t start from zero. They start from the last ten migrations your org ran.

The internal consultant IDP is the tooling layer your consultants will use during the engagement.

Neither of the two layers is client-facing. But both directly improve what the client experiences with faster delivery, better decisions, consistent outcomes across every engagement.

Building a capability layer seems straightforward, but service-based companies rarely get there. Here are the three reasons service organization fails to build capability layer:

Someone owns the platform in a product company. They have a charter, a roadmap and sometimes a dedicated team. Their job is to make the platform better, and they’re measured on it.

In a services company, nobody owns the capability layer. Delivery leads are focused on engagements. Practice leads are spread across various accounts. Senior engineers who could build this are always either billable or between projects. This results in the capability layer becoming everyone’s second priority.

Without an owner, nothing compounds. Things get built once, never maintained, and eventually abandoned.

In a product-based company, the platform team builds the platform for stability. The same developers use the platform daily, adoption grows over time and the team gets feedback loops that help them continuously improve the platform.

Consultants don’t work that way. A consultant rolls onto a new engagement with two days to get productive. They don’t have time to learn and understand a complex internal system. They need:

A capability layer designed for a stable internal team will fail in a services context. The design constraint is completely different.

Services based companies are focused on delivery. The incentive structure, the culture, the way performance is measured - all of it points toward delivery. Billable work is valued, and internal capability building is not.

As long as contributing to the capability layer is seen separate from delivery, it won’t happen consistently. The consultants who could build the best patterns are always the ones most in demand on client engagements. And this affects the internal work that is needed to build and maintain the capability layer.

One of the things that we often discuss within the platform engineering community is how do we track and improve adoption. One of the metrics that always makes it to the discussion is DORA metrics (DevOps Research and Assessment).

Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and mean time to recovery are the metrics that get tracked, and frankly these are meaningful numbers for a product company where engineering velocity maps directly to business outcomes.

For a service-based company, it’s completely different. A CTO or a delivery VP isn’t asking how fast your internal deployments are. They are interested in knowing whether engagements are profitable or not.

Hence, the platform engineering metrics that actually matter for a service company look different:

For service companies, these metrics get internal capability investment approved.

A services org that builds and maintains a capability layer builds institutional knowledge that individual talent can’t replicate. The consultant who joins your Kubernetes practice inherits the patterns from twenty prior engagements, not just the memory of who worked there before. That's the competitive advantage for the organization.

Any service company can hire a strong consultant, but only a few can build a system that makes every consultant stronger the moment they join. That’s the difference a capability layer can make over time. Every pattern is tested, every reference architecture is refined, every decision is documented to make sure the next engagement a little faster, a little more consistent and a little more profitable than the one before.

Platform engineering isn’t a universal implementation pattern, it’s an organizational optimization strategy. Product companies optimize for consistency. Service companies optimize for adaptability.

The blind spot in platform engineering discussion isn’t a reason to ignore the discipline. It’s a reason to build your own version of it.

If this resonates and you’re figuring out what this looks like for your organization, connect with me on LinkedIn. And if you’re building or scaling a delivery practice and want to think through the capability layer model, the Improving team would be glad to talk.

#9740. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section

#9739. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9737. 505,000 Chinese characters, 3 MB APK: shipping a classical text as an offline reader

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at q1z2q3-debug.github.io

I have been writing a commentary on the Yijing (Book of Changes) for a while. It ended up at 72 sections, 505,000 non-whitespace Chinese characters, and 704 A4 pages. At that point the interesting question stopped being "what does it say" and became "how does somebody actually read the thing" — on a phone, on a train, with no network.

This post is the build log: one Markdown source, four deliverables, and the parts that broke.

Repo: q1z2q3-debug/daokedao-yijing · Reading site: q1z2q3-debug.github.io/daokedao-yijing

One source of truth (book/*.md), four outputs that must never drift:

The rule I settled on: the HTML is the artifact, everything else derives from it. The APK is not a second implementation — it is that exact file plus fonts.

The reading page was originally pulling a webfont from a CDN. Fine online, useless on a plane. So the build step rewrites the page and inlines a subset:

Result: zero external references left in the file, fonts embedded as base64, 1.75 MB, opens from file:// with the network switched off.

Android Studio was not available in the environment, and honestly a WebView shell does not need it. Six steps:

The manifest has zero permissions — not even INTERNET:

and the shell adds setBlockNetworkLoads(true) so a stray in the content cannot phone home either. Version code 15000 = version 1.50.0 encoded, so the next release is 15100 and installs over it with the same signing key.

This is the part that matters if you ever publish a long text on the web.

A single page containing the entire book is a terrible search target: one , no <meta name="description">, no canonical, and nothing to rank for a query like "未济卦 解读". So the site build splits the same HTML on its <h1> boundaries and wraps each section in a template:</p> <p>The whole generator is ~250 lines of Python and runs in under a second:</p> <p>Two things I would do differently next time:</p> <p>The book is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing</span><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">1. What is affiliate marketing?</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">2. What is an affiliate program?</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? </span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?</span></h4><p><!--Ads Managed by AdSpyglass.com--> <span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">7. Where do I find qualified publishers?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">10. What is a super affiliate?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">11. How do we track publisher sales activity?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:</span></p><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. </span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.</span></li></ul><p></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> 14. How do I find quality publishers?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:</span></p><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">A website or blog</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Through email marketing and newsletter</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Leave a comment on blogs or forums.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Write an e-book or other digital product.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Youtube</span></li></ul><p></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">17. What is a commission rate?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Who manages your affiliate program?</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">18. What is a cookie?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration</span></p><h4 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">19. How long do cookies last?</span></h4><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Final Saying</span></h3><div><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.</span></div><p><br /></p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://techncruncher.blogspot.com/2022/06/most-frequently-asked-questions-about.html" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9733"> <h2>#9733. Valin</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><p> Your private memory for everything you save. </p> <p> <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/products/valin?utm_campaign=producthunt-atom-posts-feed&utm_medium=rss-feed&utm_source=producthunt-atom-posts-feed">Discussion</a> | <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/r/p/1311454?app_id=339">Link</a> </p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/products/valin" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9732"> <h2>#9732. How to Add Booking to a Next.js App With a REST API (2026)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.opencals.com%2Fseo-content%2Fbanners%2F1794548676605-add-booking-to-nextjs-app-devto-cover.png" alt="How to Add Booking to a Next.js App With a REST API (2026)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at opencals.com</p> <p>Originally published on opencals.com. The original stays updated; check it for the latest version.</p> <p>Adding a booking page to a Next.js app looks like a weekend project until you start it. The UI is the easy part. The hard part is everything the calendar needs to know before it can show a single open slot: which staff are working, how long the service takes, what's already booked, how much buffer to leave between appointments, and whether two people can hold the same slot at once. That logic is where booking projects quietly turn into month-long ones.</p> <p>This guide takes the other path. Instead of building the scheduling engine yourself, you call a booking API for the availability, cart, and payment logic, and you keep full control of the Next.js frontend. I built Opencals as exactly that kind of API, so the code here uses it — but the shape of the problem is the same whichever backend you pick, and I'll flag the parts that are universal.</p> <p>The frontend of a booking flow is a few forms and a calendar grid. The backend is real-time availability across staff, services, and existing bookings — plus payments. Calling a booking API lets you own the first part and hand off the second.</p> <p>Before any code, it helps to name the pieces. A working booking flow has four moving parts, and most half-finished projects stall because they underestimated one of them.</p> <p>What can be booked — a 60-minute session, a color treatment, a group class — each with its own duration, price, and the staff who can deliver it. This is your booking homepage data.</p> <p>Given a service and a date range, which slots are actually open? This has to account for existing bookings, staff hours, buffer time, and multi-staff conflicts. It is the single hardest piece to build well.</p> <p>Holding a slot while the customer enters details and pays, then confirming the booking only if payment succeeds. Slots are a scarce resource, so this needs to be race-safe.</p> <p>Confirmation, reminders, and letting customers reschedule or cancel without emailing you. Easy to skip on day one, painful to add later.</p> <p>If you build all four yourself, you're writing a scheduling engine. If you call an API, you're wiring four typed methods into React components. This guide does the second.</p> <p>You need a Next.js 14+ app using the App Router, Node 18+, and a booking API key. With Opencals that's a private storefront key (prefixed spk_), created in the dashboard under Users → your user → API Keys; any booking API will have an equivalent. Install the SDK:</p> <p>Then set the key in your environment. Keep it server-side — a private storefront key can create real bookings, so it does not belong in client bundles.</p> <p>Anything that creates a booking or a payment should run in a Route Handler or Server Action, never in a client component. The browser calls your Next.js API routes; your routes call the booking API with the secret key. This is the same pattern you'd use for a Stripe secret key.</p> <p>Create a small module that configures the client. setupOpencals sets up the SDK's shared client, so you call it once and every service call after that uses the key. Import this module at the top of any server file that calls the API.</p> <p>nextBuyerIp forwards each visitor's IP on sign-in, cart and checkout calls, so the API rate-limits per visitor instead of treating your server as one very busy customer. It skips GET requests on purpose, so your cached pages stay static.</p> <p>If you prefer raw fetch over an SDK, the same call is a GET with the key in an X-Api-Key header — the SDK just gives you typed responses. Both work; typing saves you from guessing the shape of a nested availability object at 11pm.</p> <p>The App Router lets you fetch on the server and stream HTML, which is ideal for a service catalog — it's public data, good for SEO, and doesn't need to be interactive.</p> <p>The list comes back as { data, meta }, fully typed. Each service carries its price (in minor units), duration (seconds), beforeGap/afterGap buffers and a variants array, each variant with its own price and duration. formatPrice and formatDuration from the SDK turn those into display strings. You render, you don't compute.</p> <p>This is the endpoint that would have taken you weeks to write. You pass a service and a date, optionally a staff member or location, and you get back the slots that are open right now.</p> <p>Each slot is { fromDate, fromTime, toDate, toTime, staffMemberIds, attendees, maxAttendees }, and the list already leaves out times that are booked, outside staff hours, or too close to another appointment given the service's buffers. Your calendar component fetches this route when the user picks a date and renders whatever comes back — no client-side conflict math. For a month view, getCurrentAvailabilitiesMerged returns the broad open windows so you can grey out full days.</p> <p>Every booking backend worth using exposes an availability endpoint like this. If a tool only gives you raw calendar events and expects you to compute open slots yourself, you haven't offloaded the hard part — you've just moved it. Availability calculation is the feature to evaluate first.</p> <p>A slot is a scarce resource. Between "customer clicked 2pm" and "customer paid," you don't want someone else grabbing it, and you don't want to create a real booking that might never be paid for. A cart holds the slot for a short window: you create (or reuse) a cart, then create the appointment inside it.</p> <p>Checkout turns a held cart into a paid booking in two server calls with the card confirmation in between. start attaches the customer, re-checks the cart and creates the payment; the browser confirms the card with Stripe; submit places the order.</p> <p>The Stripe publishable key comes back from start, from the store's own Stripe connection, so there is no Stripe key to configure in your app. If the card wasn't authorised (declined, 3-D Secure not finished), submit answers 402 with the code PAYMENT_NOT_AUTHORIZED, no order is placed and the cart is untouched, so the customer can try again. A second start or submit on the same cart while one is running gets CHECKOUT_IN_PROGRESS instead of a duplicate order. The slot only becomes a real booking once the payment is authorised.</p> <p>The reschedule-and-cancel flow is the one teams skip first and regret most, because without it every change becomes a support message. These calls run as the signed-in customer: AuthService.signIn returns an accessToken, and you send it as a Bearer token next to your store key, so the customer only sees and touches their own bookings.</p> <p>Pass excludeAppointmentId when you fetch availability for a reschedule, so the appointment's own slot isn't shown as taken. The store's reschedule and cancel windows still apply. Wire these into an account page and the reschedule requests that used to hit your inbox now resolve themselves.</p> <p>The full flow, from the frontend's point of view, is six typed calls in five steps:</p> <p>ProductService.list() → render the catalog on a Server Component.</p> <p>ProductService.getCurrentAvailabilities() → the open slots for a date, computed server-side.</p> <p>CartService.createOrGet() + AppointmentService.create() → the chosen slot is held in a cart while the customer checks out.</p> <p>CheckoutService.start() → the customer is attached and a payment is created for the browser to confirm.</p> <p>CheckoutService.submit() → the held slot becomes a real, paid booking.</p> <p>Everything hard about scheduling — the availability math, the race conditions, the payment-to-booking handoff — lives behind those calls. Your Next.js app stays a frontend: forms, a calendar grid, and route handlers that proxy to the API with your secret key.</p> <p>Honest caveat, because not every project needs this. If you're a solo consultant booking 1:1 calls and you don't take payment up front, a hosted tool like Calendly is simpler and you shouldn't build anything. An API earns its keep when you need a custom-branded flow, multiple staff or locations, payments at booking, or booking embedded inside a product you already own. That's when owning the frontend while renting the backend is the right trade — and the links below cover the endpoint surface, the architecture, and the typed SDK.</p> <p>Yes, but you're then building a scheduling engine: real-time availability across staff and services, buffer logic, race-safe slot holding, and payment-to-booking handoff. For a single service with no payments that's doable in a weekend. For anything with multiple staff, locations, or paid bookings, the availability and concurrency logic is where most of the effort goes — which is what an API removes.</p> <p>Server-side only — in an environment variable read by Route Handlers or Server Actions. A storefront key can create real bookings and charges, so it must never ship in a client bundle. The browser calls your own Next.js API routes; those routes call the booking API with the secret key.</p> <p>Yes. Public reads like the service catalog fit Server Components and stream as HTML, which is good for SEO. Anything that mutates — cart, checkout, reschedule — goes in Route Handlers or Server Actions so the secret key stays on the server.</p> <p>A calendar API stores and returns events. A booking API computes availability — it knows service durations, staff assignments, buffers, and existing bookings, and returns the slots a customer can actually book. With a calendar API you'd still have to write all of that logic yourself on top of raw events.</p> <p>Yes. The customer signs in through the API (AuthService.signIn returns an access token), and your server calls AppointmentService.list, reschedule and cancel with that token as a Bearer header next to the store key, so each customer only sees their own bookings. The store's reschedule and cancel windows still apply. Wire them into an account page and the change requests you'd otherwise answer by email resolve themselves.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/stangineer/how-to-add-booking-to-a-nextjs-app-with-a-rest-api-2026-3pi" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9731"> <h2>#9731. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/sites/default/files/2026-09/400968%20Baker%27s%20Reserve%20Bread%20Flour_Spring%20Lifestyle%20Direct_2027_Shot%201_H_2674.jpg" alt="What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour." style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.</p> <p>The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.</p> <p>To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.</p> <p>High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.</p> <p>High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.</p> <p>You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.</p> <p>Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.</p> <p>If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.</p> <p>Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.</p> <p>Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.</p> <p>Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.</p> <p>Cover photo by Patrick Marinello; food styling by Yekaterina Boytsova.</p> <p>Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.</p> <p>Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.</p> <p>See our complete collection of Story posts.</p> <p>Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.</p> <p>Don’t fall for this classic sourdough starter trick.</p> <p>Facebook TikTok Instagram Threads Pinterest LinkedIn YouTube Reddit Substack</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2026/09/28/what-is-high-extraction-flour" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9730"> <h2>#9730.
