Questions?</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/08/260814235856.htm" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9580"> <h2>#9580. 1-Bowl Honey Almond Snack Cake (Gluten-Free)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Gluten-Free-Honey-Cake-15-683x1024.jpg" alt="1-Bowl Honey Almond Snack Cake (Gluten-Free)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Honey almond snack cake!? You know you want to jump in on the fun! This GORGEOUS loaf is perfectly moist with a lightly floral flavor and beautiful sponge texture. Bonus? It’s made without gluten or dairy, but no one will know.</p> <p>It’s the perfect cake for afternoon tea, brunch gatherings, and beyond! Just 10 ingredients, 1 bowl, and simple methods (no mixer) required. Let’s bake!</p> <p>This light, fluffy gluten-free honey almond cake is made with 10 simple ingredients:</p> <p>After mixing together your wet ingredients, then adding your dry ingredients, it’s time to pour the batter into a parchment-lined loaf pan. The parchment paper will prevent sticking and make it super easy to remove the cake from the pan.</p> <p>We also think this cake would work beautifully in an 8-inch round cake pan, but it will bake much faster!</p> <p>Top with sliced almonds before baking, then pop that beauty in the oven! After baking and letting the cake cool slightly, we love to add an extra drizzle of honey. Deliciousness awaits, friends!</p> <p>We hope you LOVE this honey almond cake! It’s:FluffyFloralSpongySubtly sweetPerfectly moist& SO delicious!</p> <p>Grab a slice of cake, pour yourself a mug of coffee or tea, kick back, and get your snack on! It would also pair well with Earl Grey Tea, our Lemon Ginger Jasmine Iced Tea, or a Cinnamon Vanilla Dandelion Tea Latte.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>Can this be made without honey? If so, what would be the substitute?</p> <p>Hi Jessica, perhaps agave or maple syrup, but we haven’t tested with those alternatives. The flavor will vary, especially if using maple. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>wow – I absolutely loved this! Incredible flavor and very tender crumb… I can’t believe this combo of pantry ingredients could produce such a fantastic GF cake. And full disclosure – I was kind of winging it with what I had, so I made a version of GF flour with potato starch, white rice flour, sourgum flour and oat flour, and I only had whole almonds so I chopped them roughly for the top. I baked it in my air fryer – a total experiment, and I had to cover it with foil after 10 minutes (did it in an 8×8 pan) – and while it didn’t come out perfectly (it cooked a little unevenly), it was utterly delicious! So moist, with the browned sides and beautifully browned almonds (a benefit of the air fryer, maybe). All to say – this recipe is very adaptable and honestly so so scrumptious. I just had to tell you!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Ann! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo</p> <p>Could I use almond meal instead of almond flour? Or would the change in texture be too drastic?</p> <p>Hey Serena! We think it would work, but the flavor and texture might change a bit! Let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Honey almond snack cake looks like the perfect simple bake. Appreciate how approachable the steps stay while still feeling special — trying a small cake for weekend coffee.</p> <p>I made this as written (but with butter) and it is delightful! I love everything about it! Thanks for another great recipe!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Lisa! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo</p> <p>Made this and loooove it! Came out really fluffy and delicious. Only modification is brand – I used Earth balance plant butter and Silk protein vegan vanilla yogurt. I also baked slightly longer as the core was still really wet at 45 minutes. Ended up being closer to 55-57mins in my oven. Great recipe, thanks!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Teya! Thanks so much for sharing. xo</p> <p>I made this and it came out delicious. I was wondering if I could 1/2 cup of applesauce for added moisture?</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it! Applesauce might make it a bit too dense, but let us know if you do any experimenting!</p> <p>I followed the recipe and I added 1/2 cup unsweetened applesauce. It added a nice flavor (apples go well with honey) and it made it moist. It was a tiny bit more dense, but it helped to maintain the texture throughout the week.</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it with the applesauce, Susan! Thanks so much for sharing. xo</p> <p>I made this today with flax egg and it came out beautifully.</p> <p>Some specifics: My flax egg was made with aquafaba instead of water (I had some handy from a fresh pot of chickpeas). My flour was a GF flour from my local grocery store’s private label. I baked it in an 8″ round glass cake pan in my toaster oven. My crumb was tender but a little more dense than yours (and darker due to the flax and my blend of flour).</p> <p>We’re so glad the flax egg worked, Sara! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo</p> <p>Hi! Where do you manage to find Miyoko’s vegan butter? We live in Florida and sadly I haven’t been able to find it at our Whole Foods for almost a year already!! So sad as it has no replacement! Also – I love honey in cakes but stopped using it as heated honey is unhealthy. Would maple work here if I can get the butter?</p> <p>Hey there! Sprouts usually has Miyoko’s if Whole Food’s doesn’t. You could also use another vegan butter here. We have learned that heated honey isn’t necessarily unhealthy, heating it just get’s rid of some of the benefits of raw honey. It’s still safe to bake with! We’re not sure if maple syrup would work, but let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Sounds like another great recipe! Do you think I make it in muffin tins instead? How long would the bake time be then? Thank you! /Mattis</p> <p>Hey Mattis! We haven’t tried the recipe as muffins, but we think it would definitely work! We would suggest starting with a 23 minute bake time and then checking them every 3-5 minutes after until done! Let us know if you try it.</p> <p>This recipe is perfect for Rosh Hashanah shana! I can’t wait to make it for the high holidays. Do you think that I could add chunks of apple or decorate it with sliced apples on top?</p> <p>We’re so glad, Caryn! We’re not sure exactly how the cake would react to the apple, but our suggestion would be if you do add chunks to the cake to coat them in a little flour first to make sure they don’t sink to the bottom! Then you can fold the flour coated apples into the cake right before you add the batter to the pan. They might work on top of the cake, but we would suggest watching it while it bakes to make sure they don’t burn! Let us know if you try it either way!</p> <p>I think I’m going to try subbing sourdough starter for yogurt–I’ll report back with results!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *MessageSubmit</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *NameSubmit</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://minimalistbaker.com/honey-almond-snack-cake/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9579"> <h2>#9579. TikTok Mental Health Advice Has A Serious Problem Many Fail To Spot (M)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/tiktok-1.jpg" alt="TikTok Mental Health Advice Has A Serious Problem Many Fail To Spot (M)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Young people know TikTok can be unreliable, but its design makes it surprisingly difficult to separate useful advice from misinformation.</p> <p>Young people know TikTok can be unreliable, but its design makes it surprisingly difficult to separate useful advice from misinformation.</p> <p>• Read members-only articles • Adverts removed • Cancel at any time • 14 day money-back guarantee for new members</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.spring.org.uk/2026/10/tiktok-advice.php" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9578"> <h2>#9578. Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2024/05/physician-burnout_G_1358954935.jpg" alt="Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.</p> <p>The American Medical Association (AMA) defines physician burnout as a long-term stress reaction that can include the following2:</p> <p>For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2</p> <p>The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4</p> <p>Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.</p> <p>The AMA’s 2022 Organizational Biopsy received more than 13,000 responses from physicians and other clinicians from more than 70 organizations in 30 states. The specialties with the highest rates of burnout were as follows6:</p> <p>Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. In 2023, this 10-minute online survey included input from 9,175 physicians in 29 specialties.7 Overall for all specialties, 36% of respondents said they felt burned out, 5% said they felt depressed, and 18% said they felt both burned out and depressed.8 Based on the Medscape 2023 survey results, the following sections summarize the rates of burnout and depression among physicians clinicians working in emergency medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and internal medicine.</p> <p>In Medscape’s 2023 survey, emergency physicians reported the following8:</p> <p>Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8</p> <p>Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9</p> <p>By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9</p> <p>Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.</p> <p>The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10</p> <p>In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:</p> <p>Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11</p> <p>Nearly half of female internists (49%) reported dealing with burnout, vs 31% of male internists.12 However, 4% of both male and female internists said they felt depressed, and 21% of both male and female internists said they felt both burned out and depressed.12</p> <p>Having too many bureaucratic tasks was the primary contributor to internist burnout (64%). Insufficient compensation/salary was the second-leading factor (40%), followed by a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (35%).12</p> <p>Many of the factors known to contribute to burnout are systemic and need to be addressed by health care organizations.2 However, physicians can take action to limit their stress and prevent exhaustion. The following strategies may help mitigate burnout2,4,13:</p> <p>Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/home/topics/general-psychiatry/physician-burnout-by-specialty/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9577"> <h2>#9577. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Cheesy-Vegan-Black-Bean-Enchilada-Skillet-9.jpg" alt="Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.</p> <p>This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!</p> <p>It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.</p> <p>Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!</p> <p>This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.</p> <p>Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.</p> <p>Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.</p> <p>And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!</p> <p>We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).</p> <p>We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!</p> <p>This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>Made this tonight for the first time and it was delicious! I’ll be adding this to the dinner menu this winter. I was a bit worried that the cashew cheese was going to be too runny, but sure enough, after adding it to the skillet and covering for 5min, this creamy cheesy goodness was perfect!</p> <p>I didn’t have any corn tortillas, so we left those out and had corn chips on the side. Thank you for this yummy 1-ppt meal!</p> <p>Thank you for the lovely review, Taylor! We’re so glad you enjoyed the recipe and will be adding it into your winter dinner rotation! xo</p> <p>Well that was delightful. Very different for me – my first time buying enchilada sauce. And first time making a cashew cheese. It took more time than indicated – all that fine chopping – but was absolutely delicious. A great one pot meal – thanks!</p> <p>Thank you for sharing your experience, Kate! We’re so happy to hear you enjoyed the dish! Sorry it took longer than expected. xo</p> <p>the “cheese” sauce on top isn’t thickening and is just remaining in a water-like consistency. troubleshooting ideas?</p> <p>Hi! Sorry the hear it’s giving you some trouble. A few ideas: 1) Is it possible the tapioca starch got left out? 2) Is the enchilada layer extra watery? 3) Did you give it a full 5 minutes? You can even keep going past that – it should help. 4) Did you soak your cashews? If so, did you use slightly less water when blending? We hope one of those ideas helps!</p> <p>This was easy and delicious. As the directions say, since my squash was cut a little larger I had to steam longer. I used corn starch instead of tapioca starch and it worked! This one will be on repeat at our house.</p> <p>Thank you for sharing your experience, Alicia! We’re so glad you enjoyed this dish and will be making it again.</p> <p>Yum! I love pizza beans and made it not too long ago.</p> <p>This looks like a nice Mexican twist that is a must-try!</p> <p>It SO is! We’re excited to hear what you think of this one!</p> <p>Yay! We’re so excited to hear what you think, Gina! xo</p> <p>Hi Chana, zucchini will add more moisture which may dilute the flavor, but you could try it! We would suggest chopping it into small cubes and adding in place of the poblano pepper. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>This looks so good! Can you recommend any substitutions for tapioca starch? I have an intolerance.</p> <p>Hi Christine, we would suggest trying arrowroot, or possibly corn starch. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *CommentSubmit</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *MessageSubmit</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://minimalistbaker.com/cheesy-vegan-enchilada-skillet/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9576"> <h2>#9576. Sydney's new $641m Powerhouse arts and science museum to open amid crisis</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://cdn.sanity.io/images/cxgd3urn/production/215af00001e423db05f87f8e99aabc2f6277dc8d-1750x1249.jpg?rect=0,100,1750,1050&w=1200&h=720&q=85&fit=crop&auto=format" alt="Sydney's new $641m Powerhouse arts and science museum to open amid crisis" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>The two-wing museum project is counting down to a grand opening Courtesy Powerhouse Studio</p> <p>Sydney’s Powerhouse, a new arts, design, science and technology museum that the New South Wales government describes as its biggest cultural investment since the city’s Opera House, is due to open on 7 November amid controversy and uncertainty.</p> <p>The most recent crisis is the departure of Lisa Havilah, the museum’s chief executive, who stepped down in August over allegations of misconduct. Havilah denies any wrongdoing and says she has always acted with integrity. She had been the figurehead of the Powerhouse development at Parramatta, located in Sydney’s multicultural western suburbs, since 2019.</p> <p>Some of Australia’s most powerful and influential arts identities have since signed a petition calling for Havilah to be reinstated immediately. The petition was launched on 27 October by Kon Gouriotis, the editor of Artist Profile magazine.</p> <p>Among the more than 750 signatories so far are the prominent artist Ben Quilty, the architect and arts patron Penelope Seidler, the commercial gallery owner Anna Schwartz, and Lucy Turnbull, the former lord mayor of Sydney (2003-04) whose husband Malcolm Turnbull was Australia's prime minister (2015-18).</p> <p>John Graham, the state’s arts minister, also announced that Powerhouse’s chief operating officer, Mark Wilsdon, is on leave while a Sydney law firm, Lander & Rogers, investigates the allegations. Those allegations have not been publicly detailed, but Graham has said they were brought forward by a whistleblower and touch on “governance and procurement”. Graham’s office did not respond before we went to press to a question about whether the inquiry’s findings will be made public.</p> <p>Powerhouse is part of the broader Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences, which also encompasses a large site in Ultimo, a storage area and discovery centre in Castle Hill, and the Sydney Observatory.</p> <p>The Ultimo site was the location of the Powerhouse Museum and its half a million objects from 1893 until the state government decided to distribute the city’s cultural assets more equitably across the population base. In 2015, Parramatta, about 20km west of central Sydney, was selected as the new site.</p> <p>The Ultimo building was closed in 2024 and is now undergoing a A$300m ($210m) heritage revitalisation by the state government.</p> <p>But a public petition has been launched to save the site following a newspaper report that the government is secretly considering selling part of the Ultimo site to cover the cost of the new Powerhouse.</p> <p>The closure of the Ultimo site is a cultural “tragedy”, heritage expert and former Powerhouse trustee Kylie Winkworth tells The Art Newspaper. “It’s a globally unprecedented museum demolition,” explains the vocal member of the Powerhouse Museum Alliance pressure group. Located on the banks of the Parramatta River, the new Powerhouse was designed by the Franco-Japanese architectural practice Moreau Kusunoki in collaboration with the Australian firm Genton. Its exhibition spaces cover more than 18,000 sq. m across seven vast, column-free galleries. It also has a rooftop terrace and garden, and temporary accommodation for students, artists and scientists.</p> <p>Dubbed by some “the milk crate” because of its steel criss-cross design, the Powerhouse is in good company in earning an irreverent nickname: the Sydney Opera House was called a “scrum of nuns” in the 1970s because its sails resembled wimples. While the Opera House was made a Unesco World Heritage Site in 2007, a similarly illustrious future for the Powerhouse, which cost A$915m ($641m) to build, is far from assured.</p> <p>Even before construction began, experts told a parliamentary inquiry that the museum’s riverfront undercroft would flood in heavy rain. This led to changes in the building’s design.</p> <p>During a tour around the site in June, before her departure, Havilah told The Art Newspaper that “the whole of Parramatta would be under water” before the Powerhouse flooded. However, Winkworth says she fears people within the building would still be at risk in the event of overland flooding.</p> <p>Already widely viewed as having consumed a disproportionate share of the state’s arts budget, the Powerhouse has in recent months been the focus of a new funding scandal—the backdrop to Havilah’s departure. The Sydney Morning Herald reported in August that more than A$70m ($46.2m) had been spent in the run-up to the museum’s grand opening, including A$10m ($7m) for LED screens, staging and backdrop for an immersive experience created by the British artist Es Devlin.</p> <p>Another point of contention was Havilah’s introduction of a five-year “artistic associates” programme, costing A$2.6m ($1.8m), in which external experts were employed to help bring the Powerhouse to fruition. The Public Service Association, a trade union, claimed this sidelined long-serving and knowledgeable Powerhouse curators in favour of outsider non-specialists. The programme was scrapped in May following a review by the state treasury.</p> <p>After Havilah’s departure, Abbie Galvin, the New South Wales government’s architect, took over as interim chief executive. At the same time, the state appointed former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron as a “strategic adviser”. Cassandra Wilkinson, a New South Wales treasury executive, took over Wilsdon’s role in July, in an environment of constant media reports about apparent cost blowouts in the lead-up to the launch.</p> <p>Campaigners are unhappy that key treasures of the Powerhouse collection will not be on display in the new building. The 1785 Boulton & Watt steam engine, the 1855 Locomotive No.1 and the Strasburg Clock model—along with most of the rest of the collection—are stored off-site in a discovery centre that is open to the public only on weekends.</p> <p>Winkworth says the Ultimo site was “uniquely resonant and appropriate for the display of the Powerhouse Museum’s internationally significant power and transport collections. Now the collections are dismembered at Castle Hill and never to be seen together again.”</p> <p>She argues that the new Powerhouse was “never intended to be a museum” at all but rather a function and performance centre, helping boost the local nighttime economy.</p> <p>Five inaugural shows are all scheduled to open on 7 November. Task Eternal, the main draw, traces the history of aviation and space exploration in partnership with the Smithsonian and the British Museum. Es Devlin: The Turning features five major works by the artist and stage designer. The Dark, for children, turns darkness into a “playground of curiosity” through interactive storytelling, a crystal tunnel and 100 borrowed childhood toys.</p> <p>The fourth show, Overflow, explores the care of salt and freshwater ecosystems around Australia. Finally, The Mall centres on western Sydney’s pioneering role in the global development of shopping malls as part of modern culture and lifestyle.</p> <p>General admission to the Powerhouse will be free. Over-16s will pay A$30 ($21) for a ticket to Task Eternal. All visitors will pay from A$10 ($7) for James Turrell’s light-based installation, Shangri La (Over the Hump). A 23-day opening festival will feature 179 events including Space Shuttle astronaut Charles Bolden reflecting on leadership in space exploration. Most of the opening events are free.</p> <p>NSW government scraps controversial billion-dollar relocation plan but faces questions from community groups and parliament</p> <p>Lisa Havilah had stood aside pending “investigations into governance and procurement”, according to New South Wales’ arts minister</p> <p>The Art Gallery of New South Wales has been expanded with a new building by Japanese architects SANAA, while new displays will push Australia's Indigenous artists to the fore</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/04/sydneys-new-641m-powerhouse-arts-and-science-museum-to-open-amid-crisis" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9575"> <h2>#9575. A therapy that “rewrites” childhood memories can ease fear of failure</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.sciencedaily.com/images/1920/child-fearful-eyes-looking-through-wood-fence.webp" alt="A therapy that “rewrites” childhood memories can ease fear of failure" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Certain imagery-based psychotherapy techniques may help reduce fear of failure connected to painful childhood experiences, according to research from scientists at SWPS University and the Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology. The findings were published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology.</p> <p>Difficult experiences early in life, including criticism, neglect, or severe reactions from caregivers, can influence emotional well-being and quality of life years later. How adults respond when a child makes a mistake may be especially important in shaping future patterns of thought and emotion. In some cases, those experiences can contribute to a fear of failure rooted in the belief that mistakes make a person less worthy in the eyes of others.</p> <p>Researchers from the Poznań-based Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University, and the Laboratory of Brain Imaging at the Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology in Warsaw set out to determine whether imagery-based psychotherapy could reduce the ongoing effects of these painful memories on everyday life.</p> <p>Testing Whether Memory Work Can Create Lasting Change</p> <p>The randomized, controlled clinical trial included 180 young adults (between 18 and 35 years of age) who experienced fear of failure. During a two-week period, participants took part in four therapy sessions focused on difficult childhood memories involving criticism.</p> <p>One group used the Imagery Exposure (IE) technique. Participants were asked to recall situations that had triggered fear or anxiety (the active control group).</p> <p>A second group received Imagery Rescripting (ImRs), a technique designed to change the way a memory unfolds in the imagination. Participants brought a distressing experience to mind and then imagined a "defender" (e.g., a therapist) entering the scene, confronting the person delivering the criticism, and offering support to the child.</p> <p>The third group used the same therapeutic approach, but with a 10-minute delay procedure (ImRs-DSR). Researchers designed this delay to interfere with the memory trace associated with the critical experience, potentially strengthening the intervention's effects.</p> <p>Participants completed questionnaires and interviews, while researchers also tracked physiological measures. Follow-up assessments took place three and six months later.</p> <p>All of the imagery-based approaches produced a significant and lasting reduction in fear of failure. Participants also reported lower levels of negative emotions, including sadness and guilt.</p> <p>Their bodies appeared to respond differently as well. Physiological reactions to memories of criticism decreased, indicating that recalling distressing experiences no longer triggered the same level of intense stress. These improvements remained evident during follow-ups at three and six months, suggesting that the psychological effects were stable over time.</p> <p>"The study shows that it is possible to reduce the intensity of negative emotions and arousal associated with memories of childhood criticism. Properly selected techniques can influence how these memories are experienced, making them less burdensome," says study co-author Julia Bączek, a psychologist from the Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University.</p> <p>The researchers found that imagery rescripting worked especially well when it produced a moment of surprise. They linked this effect to prediction error, which occurs when there is a mismatch between what someone expects and what actually happens.</p> <p>That unexpected difference may help loosen established emotional patterns and make it easier for the mind to replace old, painful responses with new ones.</p> <p>"We have shown that a crucial part of imagery-based therapy is creating a discrepancy between what the patient expects and what actually happens in the new memory. It is this surprise that paves the way for a lasting therapeutic change," says study co-author Stanisław Karkosz, a cognitive scientist from the Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University.</p> <p>Painful Memories Do Not Have to Stay Emotionally Fixed</p> <p>The findings suggest that imagery-based techniques can change how people respond to current challenges by allowing them to "write" new, safe endings to painful experiences from the past.</p> <p>The results also indicate that difficult memories (including those related to failure) do not necessarily have to be experienced in the same emotional way forever. Julia Bączek emphasizes that past experiences can be processed differently over time, rather than remaining fixed and unchangeable.</p> <p>Materials provided by SWPS University. No-Bake Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/No-Bake-Cranberry-Bliss-Bar-Bites-8.jpg" alt="No-Bake Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Cozy, bright, and bursting with holiday flavor — these Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites are the perfect little treat when holiday baking season is in full swing and you’re out of time and energy. Inspired by Starbucks’ Bliss Bars, they pack the tart-sweet magic of cranberries and fresh orange zest into tender, no-bake bites you can whip up in minutes!</p> <p>Even better? They’re vegan, gluten-free, and require zero baking — making them a lifesaver during the busy holiday season. A drizzle of white chocolate (or creamy coconut butter) makes them extra festive, but they’re just as delicious on their own. Let’s make bliss bites!</p> <p>Besides tasting absolutely magical, these bliss bites get their name because they’re inspired by the legendary Bliss Bars from Starbucks (IYKYK!). The Starbucks bars have a chewy blondie base with cream cheese frosting, cranberries, white chocolate, and orange zest — total swoon!</p> <p>The addition of orange juice + zest and dried cranberries kick things up a notch and sends them into Bliss Bar territory!</p> <p>The final touch is an optional drizzle of melted white chocolate chips, coconut butter, or our favorite — a mix of the two! While the white chocolate creates a thicker, sweeter, and more decadent frosting, the coconut butter creates a drippier texture and adds a more pronounced coconut flavor that we enjoy. The combination is the best of both worlds!</p> <p>We hope you LOVE these bites! They’re:ZestyBrightSweet with pops of tartnessDecadent yet wholesomeQuick + easy to make& SO delicious!</p> <p>These are the perfect little treat to make during the fall and winter months. They’ve got you covered whether you want something on hand to satisfy sweet cravings during the work week or need a quick healthier dessert to bring to a gathering.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>Hiya! I am wondering if you might have a grain free substitute for the oatmeal? My husband and I are both grain free. He has Celiac and I am Paleo due to auto-immune issues, and Cranberry orange is our favorite combo that we miss, and this just sounds heavenly and treat like.</p> <p>Hi Wendy, we would suggest trying a lesser amount of coconut flour (maybe 1/4 cup?). Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>I have been recently enjoying making some of your energy and bliss bites as it feels like an accessible form of sweetness and energy for a snack to keep us going through the day! I was soooooo stoked to see this version in my inbox! (one of the best coffee shop produced dessert bar for sure and one of my fave flavour profiles this time of year!)</p> <p>Will be trying very soon, though I am thinking of blitzing the white chocolate slightly and folding them in! Will report back.</p> <p>Aw, we’re so happy to hear you’ve been enjoying snacking on our energy bites, Dev! We agree – it’s hard to beat the deliciousness of those Starbucks bars and the tart-sweet flavor of cranberry orange is so lovely this time of year. Excited to hear what you think of this version! xo</p> <p>If I want to share these at work, will they soften again once they’re out of the refrigerator?</p> <p>Hi Kathy, Yes, they will soften a bit at room temperature due to the coconut oil, unless perhaps the room is super cold!</p> <p>For zero coconut flavor, you can use refined coconut oil and white chocolate for the frosting!</p> <p>Hi Tasie, we don’t think they would bake super well due to the ratio of ingredients here, but let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *CommentSubmit</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *WebsiteSubmit</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://minimalistbaker.com/cranberry-bliss-bites/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9573"> <h2>#9573. Scientists reveal how the brain changes its connections when uncertainty strikes</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.sciencedaily.com/images/1920/digital-brain-connections-signal-map.webp" alt="Scientists reveal how the brain changes its connections when uncertainty strikes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>The human brain is continuously processing enormous amounts of information. Even something as familiar as driving requires several mental tasks at once. The brain must remember the route, recall how to control the vehicle, and respond to unexpected developments such as a road closure or shifting traffic conditions.</p> <p>A brain network known as the frontoparietal cortex plays a major role in managing this flow of information. It receives signals from throughout the brain, determines which information is most important, and helps coordinate the appropriate response.</p> <p>New research from the University of Iowa offers a more detailed look at how this system works when people face uncertainty while making decisions. The findings show how the frontoparietal cortex helps organize information and coordinate responses involving both the brain and the body.</p> <p>University of Iowa researchers have provided new insight into the brain's information hub, known as the frontoparietal cortex. In this illustration, colored areas identify frontoparietal regions that track uncertainty as participants encounter changes in associations they had previously learned. Image courtesy of Kai Hwang lab, University of Iowa.</p> <p>Using experiments that combined computational modeling with brain imaging, the researchers found that the frontoparietal cortex does not communicate with the rest of the brain in a fixed way. Instead, its connections shift according to the type of information required during different stages of a decision.</p> <p>The results could help guide future investigations into neurological and psychiatric conditions in which this information exchange may function differently, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and schizophrenia.</p> <p>"Our study shows in more detail how the frontoparietal cortex operates -- what kind of information it extracts from other systems and how it uses its connectivity pattern to integrate information that is coming in from different areas of the brain," says Kai Hwang, associate professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences and the study's corresponding author. "That's the main contribution."</p> <p>Scientists have long recognized the frontoparietal cortex as an important part of decision making. Its role resembles that of an air traffic controller overseeing a crowded airport. It continually receives information from other brain regions, but it does more than simply collect those signals. Depending on the situation, it filters out some information while giving greater attention to signals that are more relevant.</p> <p>Building a Big Picture From Incomplete Information</p> <p>In a study published in 2025, Hwang and his colleagues found that the frontoparietal cortex develops an ongoing high-level summary of information arriving from elsewhere in the brain. It evaluates incoming signals, including information that may be incomplete or uncertain, combines them into a more useful overall representation, and then helps direct other brain regions toward an appropriate response.</p> <p>"It's like where other areas of the brain don't have all the information, so they send what they have to the frontoparietal cortex for guidance," Hwang explains.</p> <p>The new research extended those findings by examining how adaptable the frontoparietal cortex is. Specifically, the scientists wanted to understand how its interactions with other brain regions change as the demands of a problem or situation change.</p> <p>To investigate this, the team recruited 38 participants between ages 18 and 35. Participants learned connections between different combinations of colors, faces, and scenes and particular responses. Those responses included pressing a button using either the index or middle finger on either hand.</p> <p>The researchers later altered the learned pairings. Participants therefore had to recognize that the associations had changed, learn the new ones, and respond with the correct button using the appropriate hand and finger.</p> <p>Changing the instructions introduced uncertainty into the task. That allowed the researchers to observe how the frontoparietal cortex changed its connections with other brain systems as participants tried to determine what had happened.</p> <p>"If they always get it right, they know they've made the correct association, but once they start doing it wrong, they will have to guess, 'Oh, did the context change, or did I not see the color clearly?' That creates uncertainty," Hwang says.</p> <p>The team combined behavioral data from the experiments with functional MRI scans. Using those results, the researchers developed a computational model that separated signals coming from different areas of the brain and revealed how the frontoparietal cortex brought that information together.</p> <p>"Rather than simply becoming more active during difficult tasks, we observed how this network dynamically changes how it communicates with other brain regions depending on what information is needed at each stage of a decision," Hwang says.</p> <p>The results suggest that challenging decisions are not handled simply by increasing activity within this network. Instead, the frontoparietal cortex appears to adjust which brain regions it communicates with according to the information needed at that particular moment.</p> <p>Possible Links to ADHD and Other Disorders</p> <p>The findings could eventually contribute to research on psychiatric disorders that make it harder for people to adjust their behavior when circumstances change. Examples can include speaking too loudly in a library or struggling to control impulses, difficulties that can occur with ADHD.</p> <p>"These are situations where people struggle with regulating their behavior. That, to me, is an integration problem. If that integration function is not working properly, then that could very likely mean they didn't use the right context to regulate their behavior," Hwang says.</p> <p>Stephanie Leach, a sixth-year graduate student in Hwang's lab, contributed to the design of the project, led the experiments conducted with participants, and co-led preparation of the manuscript.</p> <p>"Having the opportunity to conduct this research has been especially rewarding because it has allowed me to contribute to answering questions about the most fascinating, mysterious, and complex system we know -- the human brain," says Leach, who is the study's first author.</p> <p>The study, "Frontoparietal hub connectivity integrates information from multiple sources," was published in the Journal of Neuroscience.</p> <p>Other contributors include Jiefeng Jiang, who led the computational modeling, and Shannon Stokes. Both are members of the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.</p> <p>Funding for the research came from the National Institute of Mental Health and the Iowa Neuroscience Institute.</p> <p>Materials provided by University of Iowa.
